# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The people of Grey Shutters departed for home following Christmas, Thirza having made a binding promise to come back for four weeks during the spring season. Additional snow arrived prior to New Year’s, freezing the harbor completely, yet past the pale, trapped fields, the gulf remained open. A bright, freezing, glaring winter day marked the final day of the old year, striking us with its radiance and forcing us to admire it while failing to win our affection. The sky appeared keen and blue; the snow diamonds glinted relentlessly; the naked trees stood unclad and unashamed, possessing a sort of bold charm; the hills launched attacking spears of crystal. The shadows themselves were precise, rigid, and well-defined, defying the nature of true shadows. Every attractive thing appeared tenfold more attractive and less appealing within the blinding brilliance; every unsightly thing appeared tenfold more unsightly, with all things falling into the category of either attractive or unsightly. No gentle merging, charitable dimness, or subtle haze existed within that probing shine. The firs alone retained their distinct character—since the fir serves as the tree of secrets and gloom, never surrendering to the intrusion of harsh light.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0000 }

At last, the day started to recognize her own aging. Thereafter, a particular gloominess settled upon her beauty, dulling it even as it grew more profound; rigid points and shining tips softened into gentle bends and seductive glints. Soft grays and pinks covered the white harbor; amethyst hues stole over the distant hills.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0001 }

“The departing year is making a lovely exit,” Nell remarked.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0002 }

Lorna, Hugh, and she were traveling toward the Seven Gulls Point, having arranged with Captain Saul to observe the New Year's arrival at the lighthouse. Below the horizon the sun had gone, while Venus, magnificent and gilded, rested in the southwestern heavens, having approached her earthly sibling as closely as she can. Nell and Hugh beheld for the very first time the silhouette created by that luminous night star, a delicate, enigmatic shadow that remains invisible unless exposed by pale snow, and even then solely through indirect sight, disappearing the moment one looks at it straight on.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0003 }

“It resembles the phantom of a shade, doesn’t it?” Nell murmured. “You notice it so clearly hovering beside you while looking forward; yet the moment you turn around to face it—it disappears.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0004 }

“It has been told to me that the shadow of Venus is visible merely a single time in one's existence, and that the greatest blessing of your existence will arrive within twelve months of beholding it,” Lorna remarked. Yet her words were uttered with a certain sternness; perchance she believed that not even the shadow of Venus was capable of delivering a life's blessing to her. Nell gave a smile in the gentle dusk; she experienced no doubt regarding the nature of the pledge made to her by the mysterious shadow.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0005 }

Ambrose Kerr was discovered by them at the lighthouse. Nell initially experienced a desire to be angry about how this long-haired and long-bearded oddity had barged into the accustomed small group. However, it was not long before Ambrose Kerr demonstrated that he had a rightful right to belong among the inhabitants of Joseph's home. Being a clever, sharp, and widely read individual, he equaled Captain Saul himself when it came to the skill of sharing an entertaining tale. Every one of them felt pleased after he consented to join them in seeing the old year through to its end.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0006 }

Having traveled down to pass New Year’s alongside his great-uncle, Captain Saul’s young nephew Joe had drifted off to sleep upon the couch, where the First Mate lay asleep at his feet, rolled into a large sphere of gold.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0007 }

“Isn’t he a sweet small man?” Captain Saul remarked in a gloating manner. “Watching a tiny child sleeping is something I truly cherish, Mistress Carrow. I consider it to be the most gorgeous vision on earth. Spending a night down here is something Joe really loves, since he gets to share my bed. Being forced to share a bed with his two brothers at home is something he dislikes. 'Why am I forbidden from sleeping with father, Uncle Saul?’ he inquires. 'In the Bible, every person slept alongside their fathers.’ Regarding the inquiries he makes, even the clergyman could not provide answers. I am utterly overwhelmed by them. 'Uncle Saul, who would I be if I wasn't ME?’ along with, 'Uncle Saul, what would occur should God perish?’ Prior to drifting off to sleep this evening, he aimed those two questions right at me. Concerning his fancy, it drifts far beyond all limits. He creates the most extraordinary tales—only for his mother to confine him inside the closet on account of his story-telling. Yet he takes a seat and invents a new story, keeping it prepared to tell her upon his release. Tonight when he arrived down here, he possessed one for me. 'Uncle Saul,’ he utters, as grave as a grave marker, 'I experienced an ’venture today in the Glen.’ 'Indeed, what occurred?’ I ask, anticipating a rather shocking tale, though I was in no manner ready for the actual account I received. 'A wolf crossed my path in the street,’ he states, 'an ’normous wolf featuring a giant, red mouf alongside TERRIBLY long teeth, Uncle Saul.’ 'I was unaware of any wolves existing up at the Glen,’ I say. 'Oh, he traveled there from a great distance away,’ Joe claims, 'and I believed he intended to devour me, Uncle Saul.’ 'Did it frighten you?’ I ask. 'No, because a large gun was in my possession,’ Joe replies, 'and I gunned the wolf down until he was dead, Uncle Saul,—entirely dead—after which he ascended into heaven and snapped his teeth at God,’ he asserts. Truly, I was completely astonished, Mistress Carrow.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0008 }

By the fire of driftwood, the hours unfolded in joyful laughter. Captain Saul recounted stories, while Ambrose Kerr delivered old Scotch ballads with an excellent tenor voice; ultimately, Captain Saul retrieved his antique brown fiddle off the wall and commenced playing. His fiddling abilities were fairly decent and enjoyed by everyone except the First Mate, who leaped off the sofa like he was shot, uttered a loud cry of objection, and escaped frantically up the stairs.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0009 }

“It is impossible to develop a musical ear in that cat under any circumstances,” Captain Saul remarked. “His stays are too brief for him to acquire a taste for it. The moment the organist started playing after we had the organ installed in the Glen church, old Elder Richards leaped from his chair and hurried down the aisle and out the church door with extreme speed. Because it made me think so powerfully of the First Mate bolting the instant I start playing the fiddle, I came closer to bursting into laughter in church than I ever have at any other time.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0010 }

The lively melodies that Captain Saul performed were so contagious that before long, Ambrose Kerr experienced a twitching in his feet. During his younger years, he had been a famous dancer. Soon he leaped to his feet and extended his hands toward Lorna. She reacted right away. With marvellous, rhythmic elegance, they twirled repeatedly around the room illuminated by the fire. Lorna danced as if moved by a higher power; she appeared to be filled and dominated by the music's untamed, delightful freedom. In mesmerized awe, Nell observed her. Never before had she witnessed her in this state. Every bit of her character's natural depth, vividness, and attractiveness appeared to unbind itself, spilling over in her flushed cheek, shining eye, and fluidity of movement. The sight was not ruined even by the appearance of Ambrose Kerr, who possessed a lengthy beard and hair. Quite the opposite, it appeared to improve the scene. Ambrose Kerr resembled a Viking from ancient times, engaged in a dance alongside a blue-eyed, golden-haired daughter from the Northland.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0011 }

“That was the finest dancing I have ever witnessed, though I have viewed a fair share throughout my life,” announced Captain Saul, as his weary hand finally relinquished the bow. Lorna collapsed onto her seat, filled with laughter and out of breath.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0012 }

“I love dancing,” she whispered to Nell. “I have not taken part in a dance since turning sixteen—and yet I adore it. The melody appears to course through my blood like quicksilver, causing me to lose all memory of everything—everything—save for the joy of moving in rhythm with it. I feel no floor below my feet, no walls around my body, no roof above my head—I am drifting among the stars.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0013 }

Captain Saul placed his fiddle back on its hook, which was next to a sizeable frame holding a collection of banknotes.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0014 }

“Do you know anyone else who has the means to decorate his walls with banknotes instead of pictures?” he inquired. “A score of ten-dollar bills are right there, worthless compared to the glass covering them. Those are former Bank of St. Brendan’s Island banknotes. I possessed them when the bank went under, so I got ’em encased in frames and displayed, partly to serve as a caution against trusting banks, and partly to impart a truly lavish, wealthy sensation to me. Hey there, Matey, there is no need to be frightened. It is safe for you to return now. The tunes and merrymaking have concluded for this evening. Only one more hour remains for the old year to remain among us. I have watched seventy-six New Years arrive across that gulf over there, Mistress Carrow.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0015 }

“A hundred of them will come into view,” remarked Ambrose Kerr.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0016 }

A shake of his head came from Captain Saul.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0017 }

“No; and I have no desire to—or at any rate, I believe I don’t. As we advance in age, death becomes more welcoming. Even so, none of us actually desires to pass away, Ambrose. That was a true statement from Tennyson. Consider old Mrs. Wallace over at the Glen. Throughout her existence, that poor woman has endured immense hardship, and nearly all her loved ones are gone. She constantly claims she will welcome the end when it arrives, having no wish to remain in this vale of tears any longer. Yet whenever illness strikes her, what a commotion ensues! Physicians brought from town, a specialized nurse, and a quantity of medicine sufficient to destroy a dog. While life might indeed be a vale of tears, I suppose certain people find pleasure in crying.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0018 }

Sitting near the hearth, they passed the final hour of the old year in silence. Saul, the Captain, stood up and unlatched the door a short while prior to midnight.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0019 }

“The New Year must be let in by us,” he said.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0020 }

A splendid blue night reigned outdoors. The gulf was adorned with a shimmering strand of lunar light. Within the establishment, the harbor glittered like a pearl-paved street. Prior to the door, they waited in attendance—Captain Saul possessing his mature, complete expertise, Ambrose Kerr amidst his energetic yet vacant middle age, Hugh and Nell bearing their cherished recollections and delicate aspirations, Lorna burdened by her history of deprived years and her bleak destiny. Twelve was chimed by the clock situated upon the small shelf over the hearth.
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0021 }

“Welcome, New Year,” said Captain Saul, making a deep bow as the final chime faded. “I wish you all the finest year you have ever known, mates. It is my belief that anything the New Year delivers to us will be the finest the Great Captain provides for us—and one way or another every one of us will reach a safe haven.”
{: #nw-v04-c16-p0022 }
